area.title: Meaning Ridge
area.subtitle: Mind, duty, meaning, and beauty
area.blurb: The trail turns inward: why do we know good, and why does beauty wound us?
area.intro: The path ends — and does not end — on a lookout where the whole town lies below. Here the clues are closer than stars: conscience, consciousness, the ache for meaning, the strange authority of beauty.

These are not laboratory instruments. They are the conditions under which any instrument is used. Ignore them, and the case for God is thinner than it should be. Inflate them, and you preach at a wound instead of thinking with it.
Take each as a signpost. Signposts do not drag you. They tell you a country may be real.

lesson.title: The grain of duty
lesson.idea: duty feels real, not like a taste for tea

journal.title: The moral grain of the world
journal.body: Duty presents itself as more than taste. A good God is the ground of a good law — the home that fits. Romans 2 treats that knowledge as widely shared, which is why injustice still has a name.
Romans 2:14–15 treats moral knowledge as widely shared. That is why strangers can still accuse one another of injustice and expect the accusation to mean something.

lesson.title: The inside of mind
lesson.idea: inner experience is not captured by a scan
lesson.claim: A story of the world must find a home for mind — including the storyteller.
lesson.plain: Inner experience is not captured by a scan.
lesson.source: The hard problem; classical theism on intellect

journal.title: The inside of mind
journal.body: Qualia, aboutness, the hard problem, and the norm of reason are not parlor tricks. They are what it is like to be a knower. A story of the world that cannot find a home for mind is a story that cannot find a home for the storyteller.
A living God is the home of mind: not an accident at the end of an indifferent process, but present at the beginning.
journal.cite: Classical theism on God as living intellect

easy.learn: Felt redness, thoughts about things, and the pull of truth are not just collisions. Mind is at home if the world’s ground is a living God.

match.sentence: A story of the world must find a home for mind — including the storyteller.

hold.why: Mind is there at the start — not a late accident.
hold.claimMiss: Qualia and aboutness are parlor tricks.
Theism is the only reply anyone has offered.
hold.whyMiss: A story without mind can still house the storyteller with no remainder.
Mind is easy to treat as leftover steam.

lesson.title: Invented or found
lesson.idea: meaning is found, not only invented
lesson.claim: Local meaning can be built — the lookout asks whether it is also received.
lesson.plain: You can build a local meaning. The lookout asks if it is also received.

journal.title: Meaning that can be found
journal.body: You can build a local meaning without naming God. The lookout asks whether that meaning is only assembled, or also received — whether the hunger for a final good has an object.
Ecclesiastes refuses to let work and pleasure pretend to be the final good, and also refuses to call them worthless as gifts. That double honesty is part of biblical wisdom.

easy.learn: Work and pleasure are gifts. They are not the final good. Ecclesiastes keeps both truths.

match.sentence: Local meaning can be built — the lookout asks whether it is also received.

hold.why: Work and fun are gifts — not the last good.
hold.claimMiss: Work and pleasure are the final good.
Ecclesiastes calls every gift worthless.
hold.whyMiss: The hunger for a final good has no question attached.
You cannot build any local meaning without naming God.

lesson.title: Homesick at the music
lesson.idea: beauty wakes a hunger it cannot feed
lesson.claim: Beauty wakes a hunger it cannot feed — hungers usually correspond to real countries.
lesson.plain: Beauty wakes a hunger it cannot feed — longing for a country the sunset cannot give.

journal.title: Beauty as a signpost
journal.body: Beauty wakes a hunger it cannot feed — longing for a country the sunset cannot give. Hungers like that usually correspond to real countries.

Psalm 19 treats the sky as speech. The observatory and the lookout are the same ridge at two hours of the day: measurement at dusk, longing after dark. The trail is unending because the object, if real, is not smaller than a game.
journal.cite: C. S. Lewis, “The Weight of Glory”; Surprised by Joy
